subject: Agriculture
title: The Obesity Epidemic
description: A fast breakdown of The Obesity Epidemic for builders.

hook.text: More people now die from eating too much than too little. Obesity kills 4 million people annually.

buildup.text: Ultra-processed foods—engineered for craving—are cheap, convenient, and everywhere. They dominate diets globally.

discovery.text: In the US, ultra-processed foods provide 60% of calories. In Brazil and India, the share is rising rapidly.

twist.text: The obesity crisis is hitting developing countries hardest—Pacific Islands and the Middle East now top global rates.

climax.text: Obesity-related disease costs the global economy $2 trillion annually—more than armed conflict or smoking.

punchline.text: The food system solved hunger—and replaced it with a new epidemic.

quiz.question: How much does obesity-related disease cost the global economy annually?

details.summary: The obesity epidemic describes the dramatic global rise in overweight and obesity over the past 50 years. This topic explores how agricultural subsidies, processed food marketing, and changing food systems transformed diets and drove a worldwide health crisis.
details.whyItMatters: Obesity now kills more people than hunger. The food system that solved calorie scarcity created a new crisis of cheap, ultra-processed, calorie-dense foods that overwhelm human biology.
takeaways: Over one billion people worldwide are now classified as obese
Ultra-processed foods make up over 50% of calories consumed in many rich countries
Agricultural subsidies for corn and soy make processed ingredients artificially cheap

faq.question: How did the food system contribute to the obesity epidemic?
faq.answer: Agricultural subsidies lowered the cost of corn, soy, and sugar, making processed food calories extremely cheap. Marketing and portion sizes expanded while physical activity declined, creating an environment that promotes overconsumption.

faq.question: Why is obesity considered a food system problem, not just individual behavior?
faq.answer: When obesity rates triple across dozens of countries simultaneously, individual willpower is not the explanation. Systemic factors—food pricing, availability, marketing, urban design, and policy—create environments that make unhealthy eating the default.
